title: Automation education: Adaptability helps but cannot suffice
desc: Argues learning supports adjustment but cannot resolve missing work, geography, occupational identity or technology-sector power.

kps.k: Education remains a central response to automation, but its usefulness does not establish its sufficiency.
kps.d: Daniel Susskind's Education – And Its Limits identifies difficulty entering available jobs, rather than an overall shortage of jobs, as the main near- and medium-term challenge. He recommends education because missing skills block access to work. Greg Clark likewise argues that automation strengthens the case for cognitive education and training in machine interaction. Both place AI within a longer history of technological change; their arguments do not demonstrate that education alone can secure employment.

qs.q: And the argument that I've made is that for now and in the medium run, the main challenge that we have in the world of work is not the structural one, the one that you know tends to uh pop up in lots of um popular commentary on on the future of work, but it's the frictional one that there is work out there, but for various important reasons, people might find it difficult to do it.
qs.a: Education – And Its Limits (Gresham College, The Future of Work series) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: and uh and obviously kind of interacting with machines is something that requires skills and abilities and and training  >> but there's also an aspect uh in which  things move fast.
qs.a: Greg Clark: From Middlesbrough To Minister · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Task-level analysis challenges the assumption that technological progress benefits every worker and merely increases the premium on education.
kps.d: The Economics of Work and Technology describes a skill-biased account that supported expanding advanced education, illustrated by Clinton, Blair and Obama. The lecturer argues that difficulties among middle-skilled workers, traced to the 1980s, and later apparent absolute wage declines at the bottom challenge that account. He instead distinguishes tasks from whole jobs and substitution from complementarity, without establishing which force will dominate. The supplied material offers qualitative historical observations, not quantified estimates of displacement or educational effectiveness.

qs.q: This idea that technology benefits all workers, but it benefits some workers more than others, namely skilled workers.
qs.a: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2) · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Uh they appear to be suffering not they're not simply doing worse relative to the high-skilled workers but their wages and absolute terms are falling.
qs.a: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2) · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The practical educational agenda stresses adaptability, with a difference in emphasis over when learning should occur.
kps.d: Clark prioritises equipping young people for changing tasks, drawing on his observation that machines now perform many jobs once open to school-leavers. Susskind challenges front-loaded educational investment and calls for later-life retraining with the seriousness devoted to initial education. This is a difference of emphasis, not an explicit disagreement about whether either stage matters. Susskind also advocates basic capabilities, critical AI use, and personalised or simulated learning as preparation for uncertainty rather than guaranteed future-proofing. These remain recommendations; the excerpts provide no comparative evidence of their effectiveness.

qs.q: So, all of that I think requires equipping people, especially when they are young and their brains are most receptive and malleable.
qs.a: Greg Clark: From Middlesbrough To Minister · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: one of the you know best responses we have to uncertainty is flexibility a willingness and a capacity to retrain and reskill later in life with the same intensity and seriousness with which we currently engage in education at the start of our lives.
qs.a: Education – And Its Limits (Gresham College, The Future of Work series) · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Skills policy cannot by itself resolve geographic mismatch, occupational identity barriers or a shortage of work.
kps.d: Susskind distinguishes lacking skills from living away from available jobs and rejecting work that conflicts with one's identity. He argues that education as currently understood principally addresses the first barrier. He separately treats an eventual shortage of well-paid work as a scenario worth preparing for, not a current condition or inevitable outcome. The Economics lecture's assertion that historical expectations of technological mass unemployment went unfulfilled does not settle that future possibility. The practical implication is to distinguish barriers to accessing existing work from insufficient demand for workers before selecting a response.

qs.q: The reason though this breakdown is important though is because if you think about it, education, more education is only really a response to the skills mismatch.
qs.a: Education – And Its Limits (Gresham College, The Future of Work series) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: There's never been these large pools of unemployed people because of technological progress.
qs.a: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2) · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The limits of education extend beyond employment to social purpose and technology companies' political power.
kps.d: Susskind argues conditionally that less paid work could weaken opportunities for contribution, recognition and purpose as well as income. He proposes exploring socially valuable unpaid contributions and policies addressing non-working life, rather than presenting tested solutions. He also predicts greater concern about technology companies' political power and its implications for liberty, justice and democracy. He treats this as a separate governance problem, distinct from economic concentration addressed through competition policy, and questions whether employment-oriented education can answer it.

qs.q: And if that's right, the challenge of a world with less work, that structural problem isn't simply that people might not have an income that you know the world of work might be hollowed out, but that sense of meaning and purpose and direct direction and fulfillment might be hollowed out as well.
qs.a: Education – And Its Limits (Gresham College, The Future of Work series) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: For instance, providing people with the opportunity to make noneconomic contributions to society to do other types of work which we think is socially valuable, socially meaningful and important even if it's not paid work in the labor market.
qs.a: Education – And Its Limits (Gresham College, The Future of Work series) · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources accept the proposition that education supports adaptation to automation but cannot suffice, and collectively develop it with a more precise analytical framework. They commonly reject a simple skill-biased account in which more advanced education ensures broadly shared gains. Instead, they distinguish task-level substitution from complementarity and separate skills mismatch from geographic mismatch, occupational identity and a possible future shortage of work. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than direction: Education – And Its Limits treats education as the best near-term response to frictional unemployment while specifying its limits across employment, social purpose and technology-sector power; The Economics of Work and Technology contributes chiefly a task-based labour-market framework and does not determine whether substitution or complementarity will dominate. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally.

qs.q: Uh it's going to turn out that thinking about the world of work in terms of individual tasks rather than entire jobs is going to be a very revealing way of thinking about the impact of technology on work.
qs.a: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2) · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied regulator/public-policy voice supports the proposition’s positive claim that education and adaptability help workers adjust to automation. Greg Clark argues that mechanisation has reduced access to routine physical work, increasing the importance of cognitive education, machine-interaction skills and readiness to change tasks over a career. His emphasis is chiefly on equipping people while young, whereas the cluster also stresses later-life retraining. He does not challenge the proposition’s warning that education is insufficient; rather, he leaves it unexamined, offering no analysis of missing work, geographic mismatch, occupational identity or technology-sector power. Because this facet contains only one curated source, it provides no basis for claims about prevalence or broad agreement among regulators, courts and professional bodies, and there is little internal variation beyond Clark’s combination of early education and continuing adaptability.

qs.q: And so you both need to, I think, have a a more developed kind of cognitive education.
qs.a: Greg Clark: From Middlesbrough To Minister · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Technology moves very fast and you need to be able to do different things from from what you started doing.
qs.a: Greg Clark: From Middlesbrough To Minister · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The 2025 source accepts the proposition’s core implication that education and skills policy are useful but insufficient as a general response to automation. It argues that the earlier skill-biased framework—under which technology benefits all workers while favouring the skilled, making advanced education the principal policy response—cannot explain adverse outcomes in the middle or absolute wage declines at the bottom of the labour market. It materially extends the proposition by replacing a broad high-skill/low-skill framing with task-level analysis and by distinguishing technological substitution from complementarity. This provides a mechanism for explaining why more education will not uniformly protect workers: technology can displace particular activities while complementing others within the same job. There is some internal qualification, but not enough to make the position Mixed: the lecturer notes that predicted technological mass unemployment has historically not materialised and does not establish whether substitution or complementarity will dominate. The source also does not address the proposition’s separate concerns about geographic mismatch, occupational identity, social purpose or technology-sector political power. Because this is one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of a broader group.

qs.q: Uh, and it turns out, as we're going to see, that skill bias view of technological change, which focuses entirely on high-skilled workers and lowskilled workers, doesn't really have us anything interesting to tell us about what's going on in the middle of the labor market.
qs.a: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2) · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Uh it's going to turn out that thinking about the world of work in terms of individual tasks rather than entire jobs is going to be a very revealing way of thinking about the impact of technology on work.
qs.a: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2) · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 sources support the proposition that education and adaptability are important responses to automation but are not sufficient on their own. Clark argues that rapid technological change makes cognitive education, machine-interaction training and readiness to change tasks increasingly necessary. Susskind supplies the more developed limiting argument: education is the best near-term response to skills-related frictional unemployment, yet it does not resolve geographic mismatch, occupational identity barriers, a possible future shortage of paid work, loss of purpose or technology companies’ political power. The main internal variation concerns timing and scope. Clark emphasises equipping people while young, whereas Susskind stresses lifelong retraining and criticises front-loaded educational investment. Clark largely addresses adaptation through skills, while Susskind explicitly delineates the problems that skills policy cannot solve. These are recommendations and historically informed arguments rather than quantitative demonstrations of educational effectiveness; the curated sources should not be treated as representative of all 2026 views.
